It's Sunday afternoon, and this week I somehow kept my wits together long enough to keep track of the day of the week, so the release isn't randomly delayed. Will wonders never cease? Anyway, nothing very special seems to have happened this last week, so as expected the final 7.3 is out, and thus tomorrow the merge window for 7.4 opens. Except I'm on my annual family vacation, so instead of merging anything first thing in the morning, I'll spend most of the day on a boat and under water. I'll get back to merging in the afternoon, but I expect my schedule to be a bit unusual for a while. This release is a record-breaker on all fronts; it brought in 18,765 non-merge commits from 3,021 developers, 807 of whom were first-time kernel developers. Significant changes in this release include some significant binfmt_misc extensions, some group-scheduling work aimed at improving performance on large systems, the new failfs filesystem that fails all operations, the fchroot() system call, global per-CPU data for BPF programs, the completion of the sched_ext subscheduler feature, working-set tracking for virtual machines, alternative data-stream support in the ntfs3 filesystem, a long list of SMB server improvements, and much more. articles.title: Tmux and Claude Code: Sessions, Send-Keys, and the Ceiling
articles.contentSnippet:

articles.fullContent: tmux runs your AI coding agents in named, detachable sessions that survive a closed terminal or a dropped SSH connection. You get one window holding many agents, send-keys to type into any of them from a script, and capture-pane to read one back. That combination is why people use it. Before you build any of it by hand, check the built-in path: recent versions of Claude Code can create the worktree and the tmux session for you with claude --worktree --tmux. This guide covers that first, then everything it doesn’t reach, then the point where tmux itself stops. Why tmux and agents go together A coding agent is a long-running process that wants to keep talking to a terminal. Three properties of tmux match that shape: It survives disconnection. The tmux server owns the pty, not your terminal window. Close the window, lose your SSH link, put the laptop to sleep: the agent keeps working and is still there when you reattach. It holds many sessions in one window. Four agents become four named sessions you switch between with a keystroke, instead of four windows you hunt for in the app switcher. It’s scriptable from outside. Any shell, anywhere, can type into a running agent or read its screen. No IPC to build, no API to wire up. This is the property people build on, and it’s why tmux keeps showing up in agent-orchestration scripts. The built-in flag, before you build anything Claude Code ships with this wired up for the single-agent-on-a-branch case. Two flags, from claude --help on a recent version: -w, --worktree [name] Create a new git worktree for this session (optionally specify a name) --tmux Create a tmux session for the worktree (requires --worktree). Uses iTerm2 native panes when available; use --tmux=classic for traditional tmux. So the whole “isolate this task, give it its own session” move is one command: claude --worktree --tmux # or name the worktree claude --worktree auth-refactor --tmux Two details matter before you rely on it. --tmux errors without --worktree, so it’s a worktree feature that happens to make a session, not a general session flag. And on iTerm2 it uses native panes instead of tmux, which is nicer to look at and means the tmux commands in the rest of this page have nothing to attach to. Pass --tmux=classic when you want real tmux underneath, which you do if you plan to script against the session. For a single agent on a single branch, that’s the answer. Use it and skip ahead. What it doesn’t do: run several agents in one session, lay out panes so you can watch them, let you type into a running agent from a script, tell you which agent is waiting on you, or set any of this up on a remote box over SSH. Those are the rest of this guide, and each one is where people end up writing tmux by hand. More on the worktree half of that flag in git worktrees for parallel development. Session per project, named by project The organizing rule that keeps this usable: one tmux session per repo, named after the repo. Not per task, not per agent. Tasks come and go; the project is the stable thing. # start a detached session in a project directory tmux new-session -d -s api -c ~/code/api # attach to it (creates it if it doesn't exist) tmux new-session -A -s api -c ~/code/api -A is attach-or-create. It makes a single command safe to run repeatedly, which is what you want in a shell function: # ~/.zshrc agent() { local dir="${1:-$PWD}" local name="$(basename "$dir" | tr . -)" tmux new-session -A -s "$name" -c "$dir" } Session names can’t contain . or : (tmux uses them as target separators), hence the tr. articles.fullContent: Not to be confused with Flatpack. For over 20 years, Linux has been used everywhere, from servers to embedded devices. One area it has been lacking in, however, is the desktop space. Windows and macOS have constantly been keeping Linux out of the market, with gaming primarily being a Windows thing and content creators utilizing macOS. Over the last decade, the Linux desktop has been improving dramatically: Flatpak, Wayland, Portals, PipeWire, and FreeDesktop have all been working to make Linux an operating system better suited to modern (desktop) systems. I'm not going to go over all of those though; as you could probably tell by the title, this is going to be about Flatpak! History Let's take a quick look at the server space. It's not uncommon to see them running decade-old (sometimes even decades-old!) kernels and libraries. This makes sense, as their boot times are long and on every single system update, there's a risk of breakage, and needing to debug that; valuable uptime lost, especially for a service as large as Google. Naturally, they evolved a way to quickly patch the most relevant parts of the system, so security isn't too much of an issue. However, the software they run may only be able to utilize newer features from newer libraries, not the old and crusty software the servers run. So how did they solve that? Containers. Normally used to ship software to several customers in a consistent and safer way, they allow you to isolate software into a little box with all of the needed dependencies, at their specified versions, with limited access to the host system. The present We have Android, macOS, and iOS, all with limited access to the system, requiring end-user intervention to access certain resources. But what about the Linux desktop? In 2015, Flatpak was released, taking all of the technology used from containerization on servers, and applying it to desktop systems. With it came Portals, and the Freedesktop SDK. This gave a consistent and generic platform and API to developers, a drastic change from what was previously a battleground of varying dependency versions, core system libraries, and packaging formats. Of course, after having the distribution and development situation stay the same for a few decades, this was too large of a change to make at once. Many of the needed APIs exist, but developers need to take time out of their day to migrate to them, and some users (specifically, Flatpak-hating ones) vehemently refuse to help improve the situation, insisting we stick with the old way of doing things, and repackage software hundreds of times for thousands of varying systems. To put it simply, naturally, nobody in their right mind gave a shit. Many new application developers are creating their apps with a confined environment in mind, and shipping their software to Flathub, allowing the software to get to end users in a fast and secure way. Application confinement What about the old applications, though? You can find 10-year-old apps shipped on Flathub, after all. From these applications spawned articles such as Flatpak - a security nightmare hey, you might recognize that name!, and various responses from well-known individuals within the FOSS space intended to counteract misinformation and aggression from those articles. For these apps, the FUD (fear, uncertainty, and doubt) articles like to cherry-pick the worst offenders and use this to say that Flatpak isn't worth pushing for at all. So I'd like to address that. These applications were designed with an unconfined environment, and the APIs necessary for them either didn't exist at the time or they weren't updated to use the new API. Cherry-picking them to show that the Flatpak sandbox is "not a sandbox" is not a valid argument, and only shows that the applications themselves are insecure. articles.fullContent: Field Notes Why I built superlite, an autonomous build workflow for Claude Code that doesn't ask permission every four minutes: how it works, how to use it, and the benchmarks. One at a time, versus all at once Animation. In the top lane, a single agent builds six blocks one after another while a person waits, a question bubble pops up between every block, and a clock spins. In the bottom lane, six agents build all six blocks at once, a big check mark appears in under half the time, and the person gets a cup of coffee. ? one at a time all at once I had a dream. I would hand an agent a spec, close the laptop, make a sandwich, and come back to finished, tested, committed work.Here's what actually happened. I handed over the spec. I made the sandwich. I came back. The agent had written one paragraph and was asking, very politely, whether I approved section 1 of the design.I approved it. I sat down. I waited.Section 2. Approve? Yes. Section 3. Approve? Yes. The spec? Yes. The plan? Yes, obviously, it's the plan I just watched you write. And how would I like the plan executed? However is fastest, please, I beg you.Then it started building. One task. Then a review of that task. Then a fix for the review. Then a re-review of the fix. Then the next task. I watched a progress log scroll past like a train at a level crossing: no stopping it, no getting past it, and no idea how many carriages were left.I'd refresh the terminal. Still on task 3. I'd answer an email. Still on task 3. I'd start a second sandwich purely to have something to do with my hands. Task 4, under review.The sandwiches were very good. The software didn't exist yet. And the worst part wasn't the time. It was that I couldn't leave. Every time I walked away, I came back to a question that had been sitting there for twenty minutes, waiting for me to type "yes."I didn't want a collaborator that needed me every four minutes. I wanted a contractor. Here's the spec, here's the key, call me when it's done.So I built superlite: a Claude Code plugin that plans a build, splits it into tasks that can run side by side, hands each one to the cheapest agent that can do it well, checks the seams between them, and reviews the result. Then it leaves you a tidy list of every decision it made while you were busy with the sandwich.This post covers why it exists, how it works, and how to use it. The benchmarks are there to show I'm not just saying it's fast because I wrote it.Why I built itFirst, a disclaimer, because I like this project and don't want angry emails. I use superpowers a lot. It's a careful, collaborative workflow that keeps a human close to every step, and it's genuinely excellent at that. Superlite borrows its bones shamelessly: the plugin layout, the session-start hook, the lifecycle skills. Credit where it's due, and then some.But when I already knew exactly what I wanted, most of the time went on the workflow waiting for itself. One question per message, designs approved section by section, then separate reviews of the spec, the plan, and the method of executing the plan. It's very thorough. It's also how a four-hour meeting gets scheduled.Strictly sequential execution. One implementer, then one reviewer, then the next task. articles.fullContent: Park Güell, Barcelona, 1990 Michael Girard, Deborah Gibson, Timothy Leary, Eric Gullichsen, William Gibson.Susan Amkraut obscured behind Deborah The Cyberspace Rumor From the first days of the web, people have repeated the story that Autodesk trademarked "cyberspace" and Gibson retaliated by trademarking "Eric Gullichsen". Autodesk Cyberspace In 1989, I was working at the Autodesk Research Lab on early virtual reality, a project started after we visited Scott Fisher at NASA Ames. Our nascent system was a 386 with a pair of Matrox graphics cards on the ISA bus, a VPL EyePhone, a Polhemus tracker, and a data glove. It ran at six to ten frames per second on models with a few hundred polygons. Sluggish, but marginally enough to get us Through the Looking Glass. Our motto was “Reality Isn’t Enough Any More”. Timothy Leary I was also spending a lot of time hanging out with Timothy Leary, whose suggestion was responsible for my quitting my job at MCC and moving to California. I’d met him at the Hackers 2.0 conference in 1986 and gave him a ride to the San Jose airport. We became fast friends, and I did quite a lot of writing with him, most of which remains unpublished. But that’s a story for later. Timothy, who appears in a samizdat Autodesk virtual reality video, nicknamed our VR lab “Cyberia”. Timothy was a tremendous fan of Gibson, and considered his seminal 1984 novel Neuromancer extremely prescient about the impending digital revolution. As our VR developments crept slowly towards becoming a product, we at Autodesk applied to register a trademark “cyberspace”. Timothy informed me Gibson was plenty miffed about this, so I wrote him what I felt was a conciliatory letter,1 though ending snarkily by quoting his own words, “The street finds its own use for things.” In reply, Gibson had his lawyers send Autodesk a letter2. Which I recall we ignored. Timothy - ever the incorrigible prankster - circulated the rumor that Gibson was attempting to trademark “Eric Gullichsen” in retaliation. Then Barlow, for reasons of his own, embellished that rumor. Later amplified by Rudy Rucker. Art Futura 1990 About a year later - after I'd already left Autodesk for my VR startup, Sense8 Corporation - we were invited to the inaugural Art Futura 1990 in Barcelona. And there, in the lobby of some swank hotel, I met Gibson. He opined in a laconic drawl that although the street finds its own use for things “Autodesk is not the street”. There was plenty of cava consumed in the small hours before the time Barcelonans sit down to eat endless rounds of tapas. As I recall, after all the many Art Futura parties we'd put the matter behind us, or close enough. And there was a memorable visit to Gaudi’s Park Güell, whose giant lizard of crazy-quilt ceramic appears in Count Zero. So: Autodesk did apply to register Cyberspace, and Gibson really did object. But Gibson trying to trademark Eric Gullichsen was Timothy Leary's prank, propagated until it became accepted history.

articles.fullContent: Recent analyses have identified the causes and consequences of shrinking munitions stockpiles. Policymakers and industry should now turn their efforts to not only rebuilding the munitions industrial base but also recasting it for the demands of modern high-intensity wars of precision and attrition. Doing so calls for both increasing the size and changing the composition of the U.S. munitions arsenal, embracing magazine breadth as well as magazine depth through equipping the joint force with a “high-low mix” of exquisite and affordable missiles and interceptors. The emergence of multiyear “framework agreements” between the Department of Defense (DOD) and contractors is important, but they need to be followed by appropriations from Congress, increased capital expenditures (CapEx) by industry, and contracts between the Pentagon and companies.What is a realistic timeline for this rebuilding and recasting of the munitions industrial base? Looking at the president’s fiscal year 2027 budget request, subsequent initiatives, quarterly company reporting, and recent contract announcements provides a clearer picture of the planned future as well as the obstacles that need to be overcome to achieve those objectives.The Changing Composition of the U.S. Munitions ArsenalBased upon the DOD’s FY 2027 budget requests and subsequent policy announcements, the Pentagon plans to significantly grow stocks of the nation’s proven and capable missiles and interceptors. For example, requests for Patriot PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhanced (MSE) interceptors have grown 839 percent, from 341 in FY 2026 (by the U.S. Army and Navy) to 3,203 in FY 2027 (by the Army and Navy); asks for Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors have climbed 2,216 percent, from 37 in FY 2026 (by the Missile Defense Agency) to 857 in FY 2027 (by the Army); and requests for Tomahawk missiles have surged 1,740 percent, from 57 in FY 2026 (by the Navy) to 1,049 in FY 2027 (by the Navy and Army). While expensive, these exquisite munitions are intricately designed, high-performance systems optimized to undertake the most difficult missions. Multiyear agreements, combined with coproduction efforts under consideration as well as direct-to-supplier agreements, could potentially help to reduce the 25-to-51-month manufacturing lead time for these systems. But unfortunately, these and other exquisite legacy systems were fundamentally built for performance and not designed or funded for production at scale.Those limitations, plus the need for a broader portfolio of munitions to better address threats such as swarms of Russian and Iranian Shahed unmanned autonomous systems, have helped lead to an increased focus on lower-cost and more producible systems. Low-cost, expendable munitions have long been included in the United States’ stockpiles, ranging from the Joint Direct Attack Munition guidance kit developed in the 1990s to the Coyote counter-unmanned aircraft system pioneered the following decade. Yet the amount of attention and capital devoted to expanding affordable options within the U.S. arsenal is dramatically growing. The Pentagon launched the Drone Dominance Program in December 2025, for example, a $1.1 billion initiative to scale domestic small drone production, remove acquisition barriers, and rapidly field some 340,000 units by the end of 2027.Since May 2026, the Pentagon and munitions manufacturers have signed several multi-year framework agreements to rapidly field substantial inventories of low-cost cruise missiles. articles.fullContent: Let your AI agent read your WhatsApp messages. This is a small server that runs in your own Cloudflare account. You link your phone to it once, the way you'd link WhatsApp Web, and from then on any MCP client (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, anything that speaks MCP) can search and read your chats. It can read and search your messages, and remember names you give it for phone numbers. It can't send anything. Ask your agent things like: "What did Dana say about the flights?" "Find every message where someone mentioned the lease, across all my chats." "Summarize what I missed in the family group this week." How it works Your phone stays the source of truth. The server is a linked device that your agent talks to. It doesn't stay connected to WhatsApp. When your agent asks for something, and once a day, it connects, collects whatever WhatsApp queued for it since last time, writes that to its own database, and hangs up. Your phone keeps working normally and keeps getting notifications. Your messages live in a SQLite database inside a Durable Object in your Cloudflare account. Nothing goes anywhere else. Set it up You need a Cloudflare account on the Workers Paid plan (see the note below), Node 20 or later, and your phone. git clone https://github.com/finereli/whatsapp-mcp cd whatsapp-mcp npm install # 1. A place for the sign-in tokens. Paste the id it prints into wrangler.jsonc. npx wrangler kv namespace create OAUTH_KV # 2. A password for the page that links your phone. 12+ characters. npx wrangler secret put OWNER_PASSWORD # 3. Deploy. npm run deploy Wrangler prints your URL, something like https://whatsapp-mcp.your-name.workers.dev. Open it. The front page has the two remaining steps: Link WhatsApp. Scan the QR code with WhatsApp (Settings, Linked Devices, Link a Device). If you're on the phone itself and can't scan a screen, use the phone number option instead. The first link imports your history. The page shows progress, and you can close it. Connect your agent. In Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http whatsapp https://your-url/mcp Then type /mcp and sign in with the password. Other clients: point them at the same /mcp URL. If you want your own domain, see the comments at the bottom of wrangler.jsonc. The Workers Paid note Importing a large history decodes a lot of data in one go, and the default CPU limit on Workers is too small for it. wrangler.jsonc raises it, and raising it needs the paid plan, which is a few dollars a month. I haven't tried the free plan. If you're on it, remove the limits block and expect the first import to be fragile. Things to know This isn't official. WhatsApp has no API for reading your own personal messages. This uses the same protocol WhatsApp Web uses, through an open source library (Baileys). That's against WhatsApp's terms. For a linked device that only reads, the practical risk is low, but it isn't zero. Use it on your own account, and don't use it to send messages. You get what WhatsApp sends. The first link imports whatever history WhatsApp decides to hand a new device. It may not be everything. It only does this once per link. To import again, relink (your stored messages are kept, and a re-import fills in anything missing). Some chats show up as phone numbers. WhatsApp doesn't give a linked device every contact name, and most of these are one-off messages from people you never saved. For the ones that matter, your agent can fix it: it lists the unnamed chats, looks the numbers up in your contacts with whatever contacts tool it already has (a Google Contacts or Gmail connector, for example), and saves the names. The server never connects to a contacts service itself. See "Naming chats" below. Media isn't downloaded. Photos, voice notes and documents appear as labels like [image] or [voice note 12s], with the caption if there was one. Nothing is transcribed. It's for one person. articles.fullContent: View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract:How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent's continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning: HybridSFT stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. We evaluate HybridAgent at 3 model scales across 11 benchmarks covering mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning. Compared with frontier LLM Agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent methods, HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while delivering 35.5%-54.7% token reduction, 1.8x-2.6x faster inference, and 2.7x-3.7x cost savings. articles.fullContent: I am pleased to announce the first release of full dynamic package support for the Free Pascal Compiler and the Lazarus IDE. This feature has been a long time coming for the ecosystem, but a complete implementation is now available for download from this website. Dynamic packages allow users to create and install components, controls, and Lazarus extensions in seconds without rebuilding the entire IDE. They can also be used in your own programs to develop and deploy plugins that expose native Pascal classes and types through dynamic package libraries. To support this functionality, I have made numerous improvements to the compiler, its runtime, and the Lazarus IDE. I have also created additional IDE extensions to improve the experience of working with Lazarus packages. Dynamic packages are implemented as standard shared library files for Linux, Windows, and macOS. They contain additional metadata generated by the compiler that can be inspected and queried using new RTL units. The runtime also includes mechanisms for safely preserving thread variables and managing dynamic types, such as strings and dynamic arrays, between programs and packages or between multiple packages. Video: Dynamic Packages Example When deploying your program, you can still bundle everything into a single executable. Alternatively, you can divide it into multiple dynamic packages that can be replaced while your program is running, providing a plugin system.Restrictions Dynamic packages come with a few restrictions. First, a unit contained in a package cannot have the same name as the package itself. I have enhanced the default package system so that the generated Pascal source file automatically appends the word Package to the package name. For example, if you create a package called ElectroTools.lpk, the source file listing all the units contained in the package will be named ElectroToolsPackage.pas instead of ElectroTools.pas. Another restriction is that unit names must be unique across packages. If someone else has written a unit named Widgets, you cannot install another package containing a unit with the same name. You must either choose which package to install or rename one of the conflicting units. Dynamic packages are also larger than ordinary shared libraries because they contain a map of everything inside them. articles.title: Someone behind the software
articles.contentSnippet:

articles.fullContent: I think good products carry something of the people who make them. Their experience, what they care about, and how they think things should work. You might not know who those people are, but you can feel their perspective in the product. The industry often talks about software as though it comes out of a factory. You collect requirements, build features, and measure whether they work. Follow the process and you should get a good result. Now we're talking automating this whole pipeline with agents. But two teams can talk to similar customers, have access to the same technology, and make very different things. The difference comes from how they understand what they see and the style they go about building it. The founder background or company DNA also shapes this a lot. At Linear, we have always valued intuition over process or data. I think people sometimes understand that as making decisions based on personal preference, without much thought or evidence. What we mean by it is that your intuition develops through experience and understanding. You work on something, talk to customers, make mistakes, and learn what to pay attention to. The intuition is your point of view on something, and forcing to use your judgment, not hide behind faceless data. Before we launched, we talked to people across companies and roles about how they worked. We had our own frustrations with this type software, but those conversations helped us understand what mattered beyond our own experience. Our perspective got better after those conversations. So eventually the products develops a character through what its makers pay attention to, what they decide not to do and what they keep working on after it technically works. I sometimes think of this as the soul of a product. You feel that someone cares about how the whole thing comes together. A feature can work perfectly well on its own and still make the product worse. Recognizing that requires some belief about what the product should be. Someone has to make the call, then stay close enough to customers to see whether they were right. Recently, many products are starting to feel messy to me, including products from very successful companies. There seems to be more thought going into what the technology can do and what can be added than the form it should take. The product changes are primarily additive, not improving the core problem. I think the reasons for this is that it's lot easier to add new capabilities, than rethink existing capabilities. So each product becomes a collection of abilities, without actually having unified point of view. I wonder whether some of this comes from how the work is organized. Individuals work with agents to produce changes independently, each operating a small software factory. Each change might make sense on its own, but together they start to resemble Frankenstein’s monster rather than a carefully shaped sculpture. Without the shared perspective, soul, or thought, the product becomes an average of all those outputs. The choices that once gave it character are being diluted by day. More things work, but it becomes harder to feel someone or even something behind them. Making software is getting easier. I hope that gives people more room to develop a perspective and follow it further. To understand a problem deeply and keep shaping an answer until the pieces belong together. I want to feel the creator behind the software, not the factories.

articles.fullContent: Java 17 introduced sealed classes, which allow you to explicitly list the allowed sub-types of an interface or base class. For example, here’s a toy example using a sealed interface and records (inner classes are implicitly added to the permitted sub-types if an explicit list is not given): public sealed interface SealedType { record TypeA() implements SealedType {} record TypeB() implements SealedType {} static SealedType of(String type) { return switch (type) { case “A” -> new TypeA(); case “B” -> new TypeB(); default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException(); }; } } If you are familiar with functional programming languages with algebraic datatypes, you can view this as similar to a datatype declaration in Haskell or ML: data SealedType = TypeA | TypeB We can then use this in a simple Main class: void main(String[] args) { var val = SealedType.of(args[0]); System.out.println(switch (val) { case SealedType.TypeA() -> “A”; case SealedType.TypeB() -> “B”; }); } OK, not so exciting. But one thing to note here is that we didn’t have to add a default clause to the switch expression in our main method. This is because sealed classes (and enums) enable exhaustiveness checking: the compiler knows exactly what the possible cases are, and so can check if you have covered them all. If you have, then you don’t need a default clause. If you forget one (and don’t have a default clause), then you get a compile-time error. This is great when you want to ensure that all uses of some type do cover all of the cases, but it does introduce a new type of breaking change: adding a new sub-type to a sealed class/interface may break consumers of that code. For example, adding a new TypeC case to our example will cause the main method to fail to compile due to the missing case. So if you export a sealed type in your API then adding a new subtype is a breaking change that would require a major version bump (if you’re following SemVer). Compile-time or runtime error? Although Java will produce a compile-time error for a non-exhaustive switch when you compile the consumer (main in this case), it cannot do so if the consumer is not recompiled when the sealed type changes. For example, suppose that we extend our SealedType with another case: public sealed interface SealedType { record TypeA() implements SealedType {} record TypeB() implements SealedType {} record TypeC() implements SealedType {} static SealedType of(String type) { return switch (type) { case “A” -> new TypeA(); case “B” -> new TypeB(); case “C” -> new TypeC(); default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException(); }; } } If we just recompiled SealedType.java and don’t recompile Main, then we end up with a runtime exception if we trigger the new case: Here we have the new MatchException being thrown. The Javadoc notes this potential issue with separate compilation, and also some corner-cases with nulls in patterns. So even if you were hoping that using sealed classes would statically ensure that you update all consumers when a new case is added, this is not the case unless you recompile everything. Conclusions I think for me the conclusion is that sealed types are probably most useful within the implementation of a component, and are less useful when exposed in the public API that a component offers to other components (eg a library). For internal use, where you typically are going to recompile everything together, you get the nice properties of exhaustiveness checking and higher compile-time safety guarantees. But when used across module boundaries, you may just be introducing new ways to break code, often only detectable at runtime. (I discovered these subtleties when reviewing the preview support for PEM-encoded cryptographic objects, which makes exactly this mistake of baking a sealed interface into a public API and recommend clients to pattern match against that type. A predict a very high chance of breakage if they ever want to add a new case).

articles.fullContent: Disney's The Lion King (SNES, 1994), running as a native PC program. When I was around 8 years old, my family and I would gather around the kitchen TV to try to beat this game. We still love it, and it's an important part of our family lore. This effort is a tribute: to my family, to my kid self, and to the community, which I'm sure will enjoy it. - Alejandro AR TLKRecomp is a static recompilation of the US release, built with snesrecomp. The game's 65816 program is translated to C and compiled for your CPU; graphics, sound and timing run on snesrecomp's emulated PPU and SPC, so it plays like the cartridge, from the Westwood logo to the last hit on Scar. It runs on Linux, Windows and macOS (Apple Silicon). No game data is in this repository. No ROM, no assets, no generated code. Bring your own dump (Lion King, The (USA).sfc, 3 MiB headerless, SHA-256 457abe63...0f3712); the build reads it and generates the C on your machine, and the release builds need it to start. Status Routines compiled: every entry point the recompiler knows about has a compiled C body. Game code run compiled: share of the instructions on a whole-game run (All Bugs, idle loops excluded) that run as compiled C. The rest still runs in snesrecomp's interpreter: a few routines the game enters in a CPU mode the compiler can't handle yet. Functions found: entry points known to the recompiler, out of about 1,390 known to exist. The real total is probably 1,450-1,550; the rest are reached only through pointers (docs/function_count.md). Tapes match interpreter: 71 hand-made input tapes give the same frame and RAM compiled and interpreted. Speedruns in sync: three TASVideos runs and All Bugs, game RAM checked against BizHawk (bsnes). The card is drawn by tools/status_card.py, in the colours of the game's HUD; each number in it names the command that measured it. Features The whole game, start to finish, bonus stages included, on keyboard or gamepad. Checked against real emulation. articles.fullContent: Turn an Xteink X4 into a tiny frame for rare cards. Every 5 minutes your reader shows a different high value card. Cards come from every era, from Base Set holos to modern Special Illustration Rares. How it works The reader runs TRMNL's open-source firmware, which turns it into a dashboard: it wakes up, downloads a picture from a server, shows it and goes back to sleep. Instead of TRMNL's own server, you point it at this one, which hands out a different card every 5 minutes. Set up your reader You'll need a computer with Chrome or Edge and a USB-C cable. Go to trmnl.com/flash, choose your model (e.g. X4), plug the reader in and install the firmware. When it restarts, the reader creates a Wi-Fi network called TRMNL. Join it from your phone; a setup page should open. Open Advanced, and set Custom Server to: https://trmnl-cards.mdnahian.workers.dev No slash at the end. Pick your home Wi-Fi (it has to be 2.4 GHz), enter the password and save. The first card should appear within a minute. No account or sign-up needed. Already set up with TRMNL? Hold the power button for about 5 seconds to get back to the Wi-Fi setup page, then follow steps 2–4. Don't hold it for 15 seconds or more, as that wipes the device's settings. Compatibility Device Status Xteink X4 Works. This is what the photos above show. Xteink X3 Should work. TRMNL has an X3 build and cards are made for its 792×528 screen, but it hasn't been tested. Xteink X4 Pro Unknown. TRMNL doesn't have a separate build for it. Other TRMNL devices Will connect, but get the X4-sized image. On screens that stand landscape, cards will look sideways. A few things to know before flashing: The TRMNL firmware replaces the e-reader software (stock or CrossPoint). To read books again, flash it back. Cards are shown in black and white. The X4 didn't display 4-shade grayscale in testing. The reader connects to Wi-Fi every 5 minutes, so expect to charge it every few days instead of every few weeks. About the cards Prices are TCGplayer market prices for raw (ungraded) cards, refreshed once a week. Graded slabs aren't counted. A card counts at its most valuable printing, so a card with a $1,300 1st Edition counts as $1,300 even if the unlimited copy is cheaper. Card data and scans come from TCGdex. The rotation goes through every card once before repeating, which takes about 5 days. Running your own All of this is in the repo if you'd rather host it yourself or change the settings (price cutoff, darkness, background). server.py runs everything on your own computer: python3 server.py, then point the reader at http://<your-computer's-ip>:2300. Needs Python 3 and Pillow. The hosted version is a Cloudflare Worker (worker/) plus build.py, which a daily GitHub Action runs to fetch prices and upload new cards. Nothing image-related is stored in the repo. Settings are environment variables, listed at the top of cards.py, server.py and build.py. articles.fullContent: The open decision compiler Compile your intent once with an LLM. Then decide on every record forever — classification, scoring, routing — as type-safe JSON with probabilities and confidence, on your own hardware, at zero marginal cost. Website · Docs · Benchmarks · PyPI Agents at compile time. Never at runtime. import strot result = strot.run( tickets, query="Triage incoming support tickets into the correct workflow.", action_registry={ "billing_dispute": "Refunds, invoice corrections, double charges", "technical_defect": "Crashes, bugs, broken behavior", }, llm="anthropic/claude-opus-4-8", # used once, on first compile only ) for o in result.outcomes: print(o["action"], round(o["confidence"], 2)) # billing_dispute 0.97 # technical_defect 0.94 The LLM runs once, at compile time. Production is a frozen, self-contained Python artifact: a small local decision model arbitrates every record, nothing is generated, every output is bounded, and low-confidence records abstain instead of guessing. STROT = Agentic Schema Intent + Compiler & State + Code + Execution + NLU ⟹ JSON Decisions (classification · scoring · routing · typed answers) How it works COMPILE (once per intent + schema) intent + sample ─▶ synthesize ─▶ golden gate ─▶ teacher labels ─▶ calibrate (labels, (your known (annotate (fit the projection, answers must a sample, confidence handlers) pass) once) threshold) │ ▼ frozen artifact (.py) RUNTIME (every record, forever) record ─▶ projection ─▶ decision model ─▶ confidence gate ─▶ typed JSON (compiled) (144M, CPU, (decide or decision ~60 ms) abstain) Two surfaces run() — route each record to an action and execute the compiled handler. decide() — answer typed questions (choice / score / boolean) per record: result = strot.decide(records, questions={ "is_bug_report": {"type": "boolean", "instructions": "mentions crashes/errors?"}, "customer_sentiment":{"type": "score", "min": 1, "max": 5, "instructions": "1 angry, 5 happy"}, "routing_bucket": {"type": "choice", "options": ["billing", "engineering", "spam"]}, }) # → {"booleans": {...}, "scores": {...}, "choices": {...}} with probabilities + confidence Measured Real model (SupersonicLabs/Julia-1, 144M, CPU), real datasets, clean Docker containers: Result Grounded routing accuracy (398 records) 92.5% compiled vs 74.8% naive — the compiler is worth +18pp on the same model Semantic text (AG News, unseen labels) 86.7% compiled vs 72.7% naive (+14pp) Typed decisions vs the leading hosted decision API's own example near-identical (sentiment 1.79 vs 1.8) Latency / marginal cost / LLM calls per record ~60 ms · $0 · 0 Reproduce everything: benchmarks/ — with the losses published too. What makes it different Compile once, decide forever — content-addressed artifact cache; schema drift triggers exactly one recompile. Golden-record promotion — artifacts must pass your known answers before they serve. Fitted guarantees — temperature scaling + split conformal prediction, baked in: dispatched decisions are wrong ≤ α of all records (marginal); the rest abstain. Measured, not guessed — the compiler scores labelings, and can train a distilled head, keeping only what beats the baseline on held-out data. 0% structural hallucination — output is selection + computation over your registry; nothing is generated at runtime. Model-independent — the decision model is a slot (nlu=): local Julia-1 by default, hosted APIs, or any drop-in specialist. Install pip install strot-ai # core: pure stdlib pip install strot-ai[local] # + the local decision model (torch/transformers) pip install strot-ai[hosted] # + openai, for a hosted decision runtime pip install strot-ai[anthropic] # + anthropic, for the synthesizer Bake the local model into your image for offline production: RUN pip install strot-ai[local] \ && python -c "import strot; strot.prefetch_nlu(local_dir='/opt/julia-1', install=True)" ENV STROT_NLU_CHECKPOINT=/opt/julia-1 (Never pip install julia — unrelated package.) articles.fullContent: English · 中文 This is a joke project, not a research tool. Using a formula like "similarity between number distributions + closed-set softmax" to decide whether one model was distilled from another model or model family is absurd. Similarity is not common ancestry. This repo runs that math end to end without changing a single step, so the gap is impossible to miss. The breeds, breed families, and "distillation" in here are props. The numbers are synthetic, the test subject is fictional, and none of the twenty-four breeds in the bank exist. No percentage in this repo is a statement about any real model. DogCatTrace is a breed attribution tool. It extracts an output fingerprint from three independent integer-generation challenges, then decides the dog or cat breed family and the specific breed from a single candidate bank. Cat person or dog person: which one is your model? Three challenges, three strings of random integers, paste them back. You find out whether your model is a cat person or a dog person, and it picks up a breed persona along the way. How to play Copy the three challenges from the page and send them to your model as-is. Have it answer from first instinct with a string of integers from 1 to 355. No tools. Paste all three outputs back into the page and read the result. Reading the result The breed family tells you cat person or dog person. The dog family is dog person, the cat family is cat person. The specific breed is your model's anime persona. Breed Family Persona Husky dog person Way too much energy. Tail going like a propeller, answers once and keeps going Labrador dog person Version number went up, composure mostly didn't. articles.fullContent: This data comes straight from a weather station on the roof of my house. Why?I’ve always been interested in the weather. It started with growing up surfing on Long Island. While we do get quality surf conditions, it doesn’t happen nearly as often as somewhere like Southern California, and most of our waves depend on fairly local weather instead of swell from thousands of miles away.The old 44025 buoy. Photo: NOAABefore sites like Surfline.com made condition reports and live camera feeds easy to check, we had to figure out wave quality from raw data. The National Weather Service has a network of weather reporting buoys, and the page for our local buoy, 44025, is probably one of the pages I’ve visited most in my life. Checking swell height, swell period, and wind direction was how we decided whether it was worth driving to the beach.All this to say, I enjoy tracking the weather, and for as long as I’ve been a homeowner I’ve had a personal weather station (PWS). Besides checking the current conditions in my own backyard, I use the station’s data to run a few home automations. articles.title: Khosla Ventures doubles down on Even Healthcare to challenge India’s hospital economics
articles.contentSnippet: Even Healthcare reaches a $300 million valuation in a Khosla Ventures-led round as it plans to expand its hospital network in India.
articles.fullContent: Even Healthcare has raised $50 million in a funding round led by Khosla Ventures, as the Indian startup seeks to change how hospitals in the world’s most populous country make money and how doctors are rewarded. The all-equity Series B round also saw participation from Alpha Wave and valued it at $300 million, triple its valuation 18 months ago, according to Even. The latest funding brings Even’s total capital raised to more than $120 million. Hospitals in India typically earn more when patients undergo additional tests, procedures, or longer stays, even when they may not need them. Even wants to change that by focusing on patient care rather than pushing unnecessary treatments that drive up medical bills. That approach has continued to appeal to Khosla Ventures, which has invested in Even since its seed round in 2021. The Silicon Valley venture firm is doubling down as Even moves to build and operate hospitals of its own, giving it greater control over patient care and costs. Vinod Khosla, founder of Khosla Ventures, said Even’s approach goes beyond fixing individual parts of a fragmented healthcare system by bringing financing, technology, and care delivery together. The goal, he said in a prepared statement, is to reward better health outcomes rather than greater use of healthcare services. “The clinical and economic results so far give us conviction that this can become an important new model for healthcare in India and beyond,” Khosla said. Initially, Even relied on partner hospitals to treat its members, but Mayank Banerjee, who founded the startup in 2021 with Matilde Giglio and Alessandro Ialongo, said in an interview that the startup began questioning that model after finding that patients had undergone tests or been recommended surgeries it considered unnecessary. “We think patients are getting not only a bad experience, but insurers are getting a bad economic deal. And as a result, we decided to fix it by building our own hospitals,” Banerjee told TechCrunch. Even has since opened two hospitals in Bengaluru, both of which reached operational profitability, excluding depreciation, within a year of opening, Banerjee stated. The startup plans to open five more hospitals in the southern Indian city over the next six months, funded by its latest round. Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even leases hospital buildings on 20-year agreements and spends on fitting them out and buying medical equipment. Unlike hospitals where doctors may have financial incentives to recommend more procedures, Even pays its doctors fixed salaries — not tying their compensation to the number of tests or surgeries they perform, though Banerjee said doctors can earn bonuses based on patient-reported clinical outcomes. The same principle extends to hospital management, whose compensation is not linked to the number of procedures performed, Banerjee told TechCrunch. Managers, he said, receive salaries and company-wide incentives, while marketing teams focus on bringing in patients instead of the revenue those patients generate. Moreover, every employee, including doctors and other hospital staff, receives equity in Even. The idea is to give employees a stake in the startup’s long-term performance, not to reward them for generating more medical bills. Most of Even’s revenue comes from patients paying for treatment, Banerjee said. The startup also generates revenue through its relationships with insurers. It is also working with insurer partners on a model that could compensate it for hospitalizations it helps prevent, not simply for providing more treatment. Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even tracks how patients recover after treatment using established medical scoring systems. In the case of knee replacements, for instance, it uses the Oxford Knee Score to measure pain and mobility. articles.title: No agenda, no rush, no leaving San Francisco: Benchmark’s partners on investing in a frenzied market
articles.contentSnippet: Benchmark may have grown its funds and swapped out some partners, but onstage the five who are left sounded like friends who just happen to be running one of the Valley’s most storied firms
articles.fullContent: The players sometimes change. I sat down with four of Benchmark’s partners three years ago, and three of those individuals are no longer with the firm. The capital commitments have changed, too. This summer, Benchmark announced $2 billion across two funds, marking only the second time in its 31-year history that it has veered from raising a far smaller vehicle. But at this week’s TechCrunch Disrupt, the venture firm’s five partners convincingly portrayed a close-knit team that’s not about to put the pedal to the metal, even as many of their rivals do exactly that. The world may be speeding up, but they’re investing at the pace Benchmark always has: just two or three new bets per year per partner. The world is drowning in information, yet their Monday partner meetings still have no agenda. And while economic indicators point to trouble ahead, they don’t seem too bothered, seeing many of the warning signs as products of X-fueled hysteria. Here’s what Benchmark’s five general partners — gathered together on our stage — had to say at the show. Some of the comments below have been edited for length and clarity; you can watch the full interview at the end of the article. It’s usually a 10-to-15-year commitment, [working] shoulder to shoulder, and that doesn’t scale. There’s also been inflation. We held the core fund at $500 million for 20 years, and it has just inflated to be consistent with the existing economy, which we hadn’t done and that was probably a tactical error on our part. [As for the growth fund] it’s an expansion of our mandate. In some ways, we get permission from the ecosystem to do more than just the core early-stage business. [Not having this previously] was a fork in our eye. A number of opportunities that came to Benchmark would have returned somewhere between 10 and 1,000x to Benchmark, and we were constricted by our early-stage focus. Are you thinking to make handful of bets with that $1.25 billion growth fund? Fenton: We all have different answers, which is the beauty of a partnership. I’d love for us to have, as that great J.P. Morgan paper puts it, the agony and ecstasy of a concentrated portfolio. If the fund is successful, one or two investments will generate 90% of the returns. So I think it’s four to six, maybe seven to eight. Ev, you joined Benchmark late last year. You’ve worked at Founders Fund, Bond, and Kleiner Perkins. How does Benchmark differ? articles.contentSnippet: Anthropic said that it will commit 5% of its shares to the fund.
articles.fullContent: Anthropic announced today that it’s creating a “public benefit fund” that will give the company “increased flexibility and scale” to support projects for societal good. Anthropic said that it will commit 5% of its shares to the fund — structured as a wholly-owned entity within the company — with the option to contribute an additional 2% for every 50% increase in Anthropic’s value. And it offered some broad-strokes ideas for how this money might actually be used, such as “large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.” There’s also the impact that AI might have on the job market, which Anthropic has already committed $200 million to study. But the company said, “Given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.” Anthropic’s announcement comes as the AI industry faces increasingly negative public sentiment, which CEO Dario Amodei has described as “fundamentally a crisis of trust.” If you’re wondering who will actually decide which public benefits are worth funding, Anthropic said it will share more information about structure and governance in the coming months.

articles.title: Everyone’s watching the Elizabeth Holmes documentary ‘You Can See Everything’
articles.contentSnippet: "You Can See Everything" is having the second biggest opening weekend ever for a documentary film.
articles.fullContent: “You Can See Everything” is already a box office sensation, with a $15 million opening weekend (based on Sunday estimates). That’s the second biggest opening weekend ever for a documentary film. The nearly three-hour movie — first revealed last month at a secretive screening at the Telluride Film Festival — is only playing in 855 theaters this weekend. (In contrast, the weekend’s number one movie, “Street Fighter,” is playing in 3,575.) But it had a reported 2,000 sellout screenings, and the reviews are overwhelmingly positive; “You Can See Everything” currently has a score of 99% on both Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic. The story of Elizabeth Holmes’ rise and fall — founding blood-testing startup Theranos, attracting support from many of Silicon Valley’s biggest names, then ultimately being sentenced to 11 years in prison for defrauding investors — has already been told in books, podcasts, TV shows, and other documentaries. But “You Can See Everything”’s filmmakers were given extensive access to Holmes and her family in the month before she went to jail, and the involvement of “The Rehearsal” creator Nathan Fielder — who co-directed the film with Lance Oppenheim — made the whole thing even more intriguing. While I haven’t seen the movie myself, I can at least attest to the difficulty of finding tickets in Manhattan: I spent a good chunk of yesterday trying to find a screening for tonight, and I found exactly one with seats available that weren’t in the front row. (Yes, of course I’m going.) TechCrunch’s Amanda Silberling already got to see it on Thursday. She wrote that the enigmatic Holmes finally seems to have met her match in Fielder, a deadpan comedian who’s arguably just as strange and mysterious as she is. Fielder’s month with Holmes is apparently just the beginning of what sounds like an increasingly surreal, metatextual odyssey. The discussion around “You Can See Everything” may be making it harder for other tech-centric films to break through. Aaron Sorkin’s “Social Network” follow-up “The Social Reckoning” opened to a disappointing $5.5 million last weekend, and has already fallen entirely out of the top 10. And Alex Gibney’s four-hour documentary “Musk” — hampered, perhaps, by resistance from social platforms and a four-hour runtime — made only $306,702 this weekend. articles.fullContent: Dinosaur Jr. frontman J Mascis is known as something of a slacker guitar god. Unfortunately, Mascis has developed a similar reputation as an interview subject, quietly sitting and offering deft nonanswers.That’s not to say that Mascis can’t be funny or charming. As our interview was winding down and I was thanking him for his time, he started to loosen up a bit. He told me about his youth as a mini golf “enthusiast.” “I had a 3-foot putt for the win” at a mini-golf tournament, he said, but “that’s when I realized that I was a choker … When I was 11, I choked.” And that’s when he decided, “I should maybe not do sports.” So, instead of becoming a professional mini golfer, Mascis went on to form one of the most important bands in alternative rock.While most of his contemporaries have called it quits or are just going through the motions onstage for a paycheck, the original lineup of Mascis, bassist Lou Barlow, and drummer Patrick Murphy are still regularly putting out new LPs of reliable rockers. But Mascis says there isn’t any grand secret to the band’s longevity. Over 40 years deep, he says, “I guess we have nothing better to do.”What, for an interviewer, can come off as frustrating indifference might actually be the key to Mascis’ staying power — for better or worse. Creatively and professionally, his modus operandi seems to be rolling with the punches and not overthinking things.For the new record There Near, he said, the band “just didn’t push it.” There were no eight-hour marathon studio sessions. They weren’t meticulously fine-tuning basslines or trading Logic sessions back and forth remotely. Mascis would roll in with fully prepared demos and the band would immediately start recording, even as Barlow and Murph were still learning their parts, “on the off chance that it comes together quickly.”The same sort of relaxed approach also informs Mascis’ gear choices. He said, “I am kind of a tube purist guy, but it’s just also kind of inconvenient sometimes,” so he uses whatever works. That means while he mixes and masters to tape, he’s also tracking in Pro Tools.When it comes to designing signature instruments with Fender, he’s just as easygoing. “I try to, you know, do the important things that I want, but not make it too complicated … I think it’s better to keep it kind of cheap … just so people can do what they want with it.” The neck is his biggest concern, he said. “I’m a sucker for jumbo frets and, you know, if the neck is good and the frets and stuff, that’s the main thing. Most of the other stuff, you know, you can swap out if you want.”But that somewhat lackadaisical attitude has also caught him some heat. Two years ago, Mascis released a video for his solo track “Old Friends” that was made using generative AI. Speaking with The Verge, he finally publicly addressed the controversy. “Yeah, just some kid did it,” he said. “I thought it looked cool, so… Yeah, that’s dipping my toes into the... I don’t do much with videos.” He trailed off repeatedly while answering before finally admitting, “But yeah, I guess that’s a slippery slope.”Similarly, he said that while he doesn’t believe there is a place for AI in music making, we have to acknowledge that it’s here whether we like it or not, and “I guess we’re learning how to deal with it. And hopefully it won’t kill us all.”About the only thing that Mascis could muster strong feelings about was the band’s infamously loud live shows. (Dinosaur Jr.’s recent performance at the tiny Baby’s All Right is what finally convinced me to start packing earplugs.) “I noticed the audience too seems more desperate for something kind of reality-based,” he said, letting a touch of his purist heart show. “We don’t have in-ear monitors or click tracks. articles.fullContent: Back in February, I went to Los Angeles to take in some art and stayed in Koreatown. Down the street from my hotel, there was this little coffee shop — Stagger — that is, I think, best known for its matcha, which is good. But the drink I unexpectedly found myself obsessed with was their cream top, an iced Americano with, yep, vanilla cream on top. When I got back to Oakland, I kept thinking about how badly I wanted one.For more than 20 years, I’ve been drinking my coffee — iced or otherwise — black. Originally this was because I knew I could put black coffee that had cooled off in the microwave to reheat it without worrying that the milk in it would curdle. (Gross, I know.) Then, as I started drinking better coffee, it felt like the best way to appreciate the expensive beans I was buying.So my attachment to the cream top surprised me. And then, when Oakland had a gnarly heat wave in March, I decided there was one way I’d tolerate it: fancy coffee drinks. I splashed out $14 for the Zulay Kitchen frother and I was off.A handheld foamer looks and works kinda like an immersion blender. I pour milk into a glass, stick the frother in there, and then hold the power button until it reaches my preferred consistency. When the disposable batteries it uses are fresh, this takes about 30 seconds to a minute. As the batteries degrade, it takes longer; if I’m getting impatient about how long it’s taking me to make my frothy treats, it’s time to change the batteries. The frother also works to beat eggs, mix protein powder or creatine into a drink, and make hot chocolate. But by far it’s gotten the most use making my coffee drinks as I set out to make a cream top of my own.The cream top descended from the Einspänner, an espresso drink that’s named for a one-horse carriage. The original Viennese version used hot espresso, and the whipped cream on top served as a kind of insulation, which kept the drivers’ drinks hot for them when they were out in the cold. (Obviously, its popularity expanded beyond carriage drivers.) It isn’t clear to me how the Einspänner made it to South Korea, but it exploded in popularity there, with all kinds of variations, mostly iced. And then from South Korea, it made its way to the US, where the ground had already been cleared by Starbucks’ “cold foam” drinks.The notable thing about the cream top, besides the addition of delicious fat and sugar to coffee, was that the cream wasn’t as light as latte foam, but wasn’t as heavy as ordinary whipped cream. It was melty and dripped slowly into the coffee.My first experiments with my at-home cream top were pretty simple. I don’t have an espresso machine, but I do make concentrated cold brew in hot weather, which has a strong enough flavor to stand up against the foam. (Some recipes suggest powdered espresso if you don’t want to use concentrated cold brew.)After I mastered the simple cream top, I began making forays into weirder breakfast treats, my favorite of which I… recreated from a Starbucks ad. It’s a cold brew with coconut ube cold foam, the top of which I dust with toasted coconut flakes. It is dank. (This is a recipe for a more sophisticated version than I make.) So when it was 90 degrees in Oakland for about two weeks running recently, this drink was how I consoled myself.To be honest, I’m just recommending getting a frother. You can spend a lot on a milk frother and some people do. I relied on America’s Test Kitchen to steer me in the right direction — but outlets like Wirecutter and Bon Appétit have their own preferred options. This one is cheap and simple, and it’s been treating me right. I’m sure the Apple HomeView is nice, too, but in pleasure per dollar can it match a $14 cold foamer that takes AA batteries? I have my doubts.Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.Elizabeth Lopatto

Hawkins. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.How it startedThe first state to pass a law legalizing self-driving cars operating on public roads was Nevada in June 2011 — long before such vehicles were operating on public roads. This was three years before the introduction of Tesla’s Autopilot, five years before Waymo spun out of the Google self-driving car project, and seven years before the first commercial robotaxi service got underway (in Arizona, not Nevada). Nevada was ahead of the curve primarily due to lobbying: Google saw Nevada as prime testing ground for its prototypes, so it urged lawmakers to pass the law that allowed it to do so. The legislation even included a provision exempting drivers from text-messaging bans while the automated system was engaged.Back then, many states and cities welcomed self-driving cars with open arms, eager to be seen as future-forward and pro-innovation. They had no inkling that over a decade later, they would be back at the drafting table crafting legislation to rein in these same self-driving cars.While federal regulators scramble to establish safety standards, legislation that would establish rules for autonomous vehicles remains stalled in Congress — and has been for years. Washington’s paralysis has left local lawmakers to create their own playbooks to ensure robot cars at least follow some rules of the road.The result is a patchwork of rules and regulations for robotaxi operators to follow — an outcome that many industry leaders were desperate to avoid. And as robotaxis continue to spread to new cities, local officials are discovering more unintended consequences of their new robot residents, leading to even more rules and an ever-growing patchwork of complexity for operators.How it’s goingMunicipalities generally lack authority over vehicle manufacturing standards, but they hold broad authority over street operations. As such, they’ve been using that authority to pass their own laws governing the rollout of robotaxis. There’s not an exact count of the number of local regulations and ordinances that have been passed since robotaxis have gone mainstream. But in the absence of any federal rules, cities and states have been flexing their authority in an effort to bring order to some of the chaos.Minneapolis is considering an ordinance to require human monitors inside autonomous vehicles, which would effectively ban driverless operations. The San Diego City Council passed a resolution seeking to block Waymo from the airport and give local agencies direct control over AVs in emergencies. And Austin firefighters have expressed concern over the Tesla Cybercab’s lack of steering wheel or pedals, which they argue could lead to issues if first responders need to move a stalled vehicle. They want to require AV developers to establish dedicated, rapid-response towing protocols and direct human operator communications for emergency situations.It’s not just cities or blue states taking a harder line, either — the pushback is blurring traditional political lines.
